And one of you asked me how you can get the cookbook I keep talking about. So this is it.
My book, Supper for One.
Forty little suppers, every one on its own page, with the amounts, the oven

And right next to it, the sausage and potato packet.
Make three on Sunday and keep them in the refrigerator, ready to bake.
It's all in my Cooks for One set, and the link is right at the top of the description. Now
§CH03§ Let me show you the cans I always keep, because you don't need twenty kinds.
I keep four. Cream of chicken.
Cream of mushroom. Tomato. And cheddar cheese.
With those four and whatever's in the freezer, I can make supper almost
any night of the year. The store brand works fine.
I've bought the store brand for sixty years and nobody at church has ever known the differ
Now, a few things about the cans themselves, because I've seen people get sick from a can,
If a can is bulging, if the top is puffed up, or if it
spurts when you open it, throw it away. Don't taste it.
Don't even open it, if it's puffed.
Same if it's leaking, or rusted through, or has a
deep dent right on the seam, the rim at the top or the bottom.
A little dent on the side is all right.
A dent on the seam can let the air in.
And how long do they keep?
The cream soups and the other low-acid ones, like the chicken and the
mushroom, keep a long time on the shelf, two to five years.
The tomato soup is more acid, and it's best within about a year and a half.
I write the month I bought it on the top of every can with a marker, and the old ones go t
And here's one more thing.
When I open a can, I wipe the top first with a damp cloth.
That top has been sitting on a store shelf and in my grocery bag.
My mother always did that, and I always do too.
§CH03A§ And before we cook, turn the can around and read the label with me, because there
The first one is the word condensed.
Every one of my suppers uses condensed soup, the little ten and a half ounce can.
There's another kind, ready to serve, in the bigger can, that you just heat and eat.
It's thin, like regular soup, and if you use it in
these recipes, your casserole comes out like a puddle.
So look for the word condensed.
The second thing is the salt.
A can of cream soup has a lot of salt, and some of us aren't supposed to have it.
Most stores carry a lower sodium kind, right next to the
regular, and it works just the same in every one of these.
That's why I don't add salt to the casseroles until I've tasted them.
And here's one more.
A can of condensed soup is about two and a half servings, the label says.
But we're not eating it as soup, we're using it as a sauce. That's why
half a can is the right amount for one person's supper. Half a can of sauce for one plate.
§CH03B§ Now, some of you wrote that you can't have the canned soup, because of the salt, o

SHOTS.txt: So let me show you how to make your own, in about five minutes.
This makes the same amount as one can, and you use it exactly the same way.
Here's what you need.
Two tablespoons of butter.
Three tablespoons of flour.
Half a cup of chicken broth.
Half a cup of milk.
A pinch of salt and a pinch of pepper. Once more.
Two tablespoons butter.
Three tablespoons flour.
Half a cup broth. Half a cup milk.
Salt and pepper.
Melt the butter in a small saucepan over medium heat.
Stir in the flour with a whisk, and let it cook one minute, stirring.
It'll look like wet sand.
That minute takes the raw taste out of the flour.
Now pour in the broth, a little at a time, whisking
the whole time, so there's no lumps. Then the milk.
Keep whisking, and let it bubble, about three or four minutes, till it's thick.
Thick like the soup in the can.
Season it with the salt and pepper. That's cream of chicken.
For cream of mushroom, cook a quarter cup of chopped mushrooms in the butter
first, about three minutes, before you add the flour.
For cream of celery, a quarter cup of chopped celery.
And if you want it low salt, use low-sodium broth and leave out the salt.
It keeps three days in a jar in the refrigerator. It thickens up when it's cold, so stir i
§CH03C§ Three of my suppers start with cooked rice or noodles, so let me tell
you how I cook them for one, because the box is written for a family of six.
For rice, I use half a cup of long-grain white rice
and one cup of water, with a pinch of salt.
Bring the water to a boil in a small pot with a
lid, stir in the rice, and turn it down as low as it goes. Put the
lid on, and don't lift it. Eighteen minutes.
Then turn off the heat and let it sit five more minutes with the lid on.
Fluff it with a fork.
That makes about a cup and a half, which is supper tonight and a little left over. For
egg noodles, one cup of dry noodles makes about one cup cooked.
Plenty of boiling salted water, about six minutes.
And for elbow macaroni, a third of a cup dry makes
three quarters of a cup cooked, about eight minutes.
Here's my trick.
On Sunday, I cook a cup and a half of rice and a cup of noodles, and
I keep them in two flat containers in the refrigerator, with the date.
Then three of these suppers are fifteen minutes from start to finish.
Cooked rice and noodles keep three or four days.
Cooked rice also freezes well, in a flat bag, for a month.
You warm it with a spoonful of water.
§CH03D§ And let me show you the only things you need for all seven of these, because you d
My little eight-inch iron skillet, the one my mother gave me when I got married.
A small saucepan with a lid.
A two-cup baking dish, and a little loaf pan.
A wooden spoon, a whisk, and a can opener that works.
If your can opener is getting hard to turn, honey, get a new one.
A dull can opener leaves little bits of metal, and it's how you cut your hand.
And one more thing I'd never be without.
A meat thermometer.
They're a few dollars at the hardware store.
My eyes aren't what they were, and I don't guess with chicken and pork anymore.
Chicken a hundred and sixty-five. Pork a hundred and forty-five. Ground beef a hundred and
I keep those three numbers on a card taped inside my cupboard door.
§CH04§ Supper number two is tuna noodle casserole.
SHOTS.name: tuna noodle casserole

SHOTS.txt: Every Friday in Lent when I was a girl, my mother made
tuna noodle casserole in a big blue dish.
And when I got married, Harold said, Loretta, I've eaten that every Friday of my life too.
Can we have something else?
So I didn't make it for forty years.
And now I make it whenever I want.
In my book, I make this with a white sauce from scratch. Tonight we're using the can,
because it's quicker and it's what my mother did.
Here's what you need.
One cup of egg noodles, dry.
One small can of tuna, five ounces, drained.
Half a can of condensed cream of mushroom soup.
A quarter cup of milk.
Half a cup of frozen peas.
A quarter cup of shredded cheddar.
Two tablespoons of crushed crackers.
And one teaspoon of lemon juice.
Again, slow.
One cup egg noodles.
One small can tuna.
Half a can cream of mushroom.
A quarter cup milk.
Half a cup frozen peas.
A quarter cup cheddar.
Two tablespoons crushed crackers.
One teaspoon lemon juice.
Heat your oven to three hundred and seventy-five.
Cook the noodles in a small pot of boiling salted water for about six
minutes, till they're just tender, and drain them.
Don't cook them all the way soft, because they'll cook a little more in the oven.
In a bowl, stir the soup and the milk together till it's smooth.
Add the lemon juice. That's the trick.
A little lemon wakes the whole thing right up, and nobody knows what it is.
Then add the tuna, broken up with a fork, the peas, and the noodles.
Stir it all together gently.
Spoon it into a small baking dish.
A two-cup dish, or a little loaf pan.
Sprinkle the cheese on top, and then the crushed crackers over the cheese.
I put the crackers in a sandwich bag and roll them with a glass.
Bake it for twenty minutes, till it bubbles at the edges and the crackers are golden. Look
The crackers are crunchy, the noodles are creamy underneath.
That's my mother's Friday supper.
About a dollar seventy, and it makes two plates. One for tonight, and one for tomorrow's l
Warm it in the microwave with a splash of milk.
Now, a couple of ways to change it. If you don't
like tuna, use three quarters of a cup of cooked chicken instead, and it's chicken noodle
Or use a small can of salmon, with the bones and the skin picked out. And if you have no
crackers, crushed potato chips work on top, too.
My grandson likes it that way best. Can you freeze it? Yes.
Put the second plate in a small freezer container before
you bake it, without the crackers on top.
It keeps two months.
Thaw it in the refrigerator overnight, put the crackers
on, and bake it about twenty-five minutes.
§CH05§ Supper number three is the hamburger hobo packet.
SHOTS.name: hamburger hobo packet

SHOTS.txt: This is the church youth group campfire supper.
Every summer we took the youth group to the lake, and the kids made these in the coals.
Half of them were burnt black and half of them were raw, and they all said it was the best
In my kitchen, I make it in the oven, so it comes out right.
This one's from my book, page forty-two, with the trick in the corner.
Here's what you need.
One hamburger patty, about a quarter pound.
One potato and one carrot, sliced thin.
A quarter of an onion, sliced.
One tablespoon of butter, salt and pepper.
And two tablespoons of condensed cream of mushroom soup.
Once more.
One quarter-pound patty.
One potato, one carrot, sliced thin.
A quarter onion.
One tablespoon butter.
Salt and pepper.
Two tablespoons cream of mushroom soup.
Heat the oven to four hundred.
Tear off a big piece of heavy foil, about eighteen inches long.
If you only have the thin foil, use two pieces on top of each other.
Lay the potato slices in the middle of the foil, then the carrot, then the onion.
Thin, so they cook through.
Season them with salt and pepper.
Then the hamburger patty on top. Season it. And here's the trick.
Two spoonfuls of cream of mushroom soup right on top of the patty.
Then the butter on top of that.
Now bring the long sides of the foil up over the top, and
fold them down together, twice, tight.
Then fold up each end, twice.
The steam has to stay inside.
That steam is what cooks the potatoes, and the soup melts
down with the meat juices and makes its own gravy.
Put the packet on a baking sheet, and bake it for forty minutes.
Beef has to reach a hundred and sixty degrees in the middle.
Open it carefully.
The steam will come right out at you. Look at that.
The potatoes are soft, the carrots are sweet, and there's gravy at the bottom.
About two dollars. And the only thing you wash is the fork. You can put two or three of th
But no more than a day ahead.
If you don't eat beef, a chicken breast works in the packet too.
Cut it in strips, and bake it at four hundred for about twenty-five to thirty
minutes, till the chicken reaches a hundred and sixty-five.
And slice the potato extra thin, so it's soft in time.
§CH06§ Supper number four is goulash.
SHOTS.name: goulash

SHOTS.txt: Now, my Hungarian neighbor, Mrs.
Toth, told me forty years ago that this isn't real goulash.
And she's right.
But in Iowa, every church cookbook has this goulash,
and we're not going to change the name now.
This one uses a can of condensed tomato soup.
Here's what you need.
A quarter pound of ground beef.
A quarter of an onion, chopped.
Half a can of condensed tomato soup.
A quarter cup of water.
Three quarters of a cup of cooked elbow macaroni.
A quarter teaspoon of Italian seasoning. Salt and pepper.
And a quarter cup of shredded cheddar. Again. A quarter pound ground beef.
A quarter onion.
Half a can tomato soup.
A quarter cup water.
Three quarters cup cooked macaroni.
A quarter teaspoon Italian seasoning. Salt, pepper.
A quarter cup cheddar.
For the macaroni, about a third of a
cup dry makes three quarters of a cup cooked.
Cook it in salted water about eight minutes and drain it.
Brown the beef and the onion together in your little skillet over medium heat,
breaking up the beef, till there's no pink left, about six minutes.
Spoon off any grease into an old can.
Now stir in the tomato soup and the water, and the Italian seasoning.
It'll look thick, and then it loosens up as it heats.
Let it bubble for about three minutes.
Taste it, and add a little salt and pepper.
Then stir in the macaroni, and let it simmer two more
minutes, so the macaroni soaks up the sauce.
Turn off the heat, sprinkle the cheese on top,
and put the lid on for one minute to melt it.
That's goulash.
It tastes like a school lunch in nineteen fifty-five, and I mean that in the best way.
About a dollar seventy. The other half of the tomato soup goes in a jar with the date on i
Make a double batch, with a whole can of soup and
half a pound of beef, and freeze one in a container with the date.
It keeps three months.
Thaw it overnight in the refrigerator, and warm it in a pan with a
spoon of water, because the macaroni drinks up the sauce in the freezer.
And if you'd like it a little different, stir in half a cup of drained
canned corn, or a quarter cup of chopped green pepper with the
onion. §CH07§ Now, I want to show you one more page.
This one's not to sell you anything. It's just good advice.
This is the start of the foil packet chapter in my book. And look what it says.
Use heavy foil, and fold the edges twice so the steam stays in.
That's what I showed you with the hobo packet.
If the steam gets out, the potatoes stay hard. And see this.
Make one muffin-tin recipe on a Sunday and you've got the month's lunches.
That's how I live alone and still eat well. Cook once, eat all week.
If you want the book, the link's in the description. Now, I've got some of your letters he
§CH08§ I read every one of your comments. Every one, with my coffee, in the morning.
One of you wrote that your mother made her butterscotch pie filling in a cast iron skillet
and you still have her recipe and still make it. That's how it should be.
A skillet and a recipe card are the best things a mother can
leave you. Mine are both in this kitchen.
One of you asked me, how can you get the cookbook for one?
It's in the description, honey, the very first line.
And I'll hold it up at the end, too.
Another one of you wrote that the recipes go too fast to write down. So now
I put up a card for every supper, with every amount, and I leave it up.

One of you wrote that you need ways to cook meals in a small toaster oven.
Well, the tuna noodle and the pot pie both fit in a

And I'm making a whole video for the toaster oven. I promise.
And somebody wrote that cooking for one is lonely.
I know it is. So here's what I do.
I set a real place. A placemat, a cloth napkin, and the good plate.
And I turn on the radio.
You'd be surprised how much that helps.
And one of you asked me what to do when you don't feel like eating at all.
Some nights, after Harold passed, I didn't. So here's what I tell you.
Make the smallest thing. One cup of soup, doctored up, with a piece of toast.
Eat it at the table, not standing at the sink.
A little supper is still supper.
§CH08B§ Now let me tell you something about where all this came from.
Here in Iowa, and up in Minnesota, a casserole is called a hotdish.
And when somebody in our church passes away, the ladies of
the church make the funeral lunch. I've done it for fifty years.
And for fifty years, almost every hotdish on
that long table in the church basement started with a can
of cream of mushroom or cream of chicken soup.
Because it's cheap, it's on every shelf, and you can feed forty people with it
on a day's notice. The soup is the glue, we say.
When Harold passed, I came home from that lunch, and my
refrigerator was full of hotdishes in other ladies' pans,
with masking tape on the bottom with their names.
That's how you know who to give the pan back to.
And I ate those for two weeks.
I didn't have to cook, and I didn't have to think, and every one of them was a little bit
So when I open a can of soup for my supper now, I think
of all those pans. That's the kind of cooking this is.
It's not fancy, honey. It's cooking that looks after people.
§CH09§ Supper number five is a smothered pork chop.
SHOTS.name: smothered pork chop

SHOTS.txt: This is the one I make when I want a real Sunday supper on a Wednesday.
In my book, I make pork chops and gravy in the slow cooker, with half a
can of cream of mushroom soup and a quarter cup of milk, five hours on
low. That's for the days I don't want to stand at the stove.
Tonight I'll show you the skillet way. It takes twenty-five minutes.
Here's what you need.
One boneless pork chop, about three quarters of an
inch thick. A teaspoon of oil.
Salt, pepper and a pinch of garlic powder. Half a small onion, sliced.
Half a can of condensed cream of mushroom soup.
And a quarter cup of milk. Again. One boneless pork chop. One
teaspoon oil. Salt, pepper, garlic powder. Half a
small onion. Half a can cream of mushroom. A quarter cup milk.
Pat the chop dry with a paper towel and season it on both sides.
Heat the oil in your little skillet over medium-high heat, and brown
the chop about three minutes on each side, till it's golden.
Take it out and put it on a plate. It's not cooked through yet. That's fine.
Turn the heat to medium, and put the onion in the same skillet.
Cook it about four minutes, till it's soft and a little
brown, scraping up the brown bits from the chop.
Stir in the soup and the milk till it's smooth.
Then put the chop back in, and spoon some of the sauce over the top.
Put a lid on, turn it down to low, and let it simmer about eight to ten minutes.
A pork chop is done at a hundred and forty-five degrees in the middle,
and then let it rest three minutes. Look at that.
Fork tender, swimming in onion gravy.
I serve it over a scoop of mashed potatoes, or a baked potato,
or a piece of toast, so the gravy has somewhere to go.
And a little green beans on the side.
About two dollars and forty cents. The other half of the cream of mushroom goes in a jar,
If you'd rather use a bone-in chop, that works too. Give it two or three more minutes in
the sauce, and check it right next to the bone, a hundred and forty-five.
And don't freeze this one cooked, honey.
A pork chop gets dry and stringy when you warm it again.
It's best right out of the skillet.
The leftover gravy, though, keeps three days in the
refrigerator, and it's wonderful on toast for breakfast.
§CH10§ Supper number six is chicken pot pie, with a biscuit on top instead of a crust.
SHOTS.name: chicken pot pie

SHOTS.txt: Because I made pie crust for sixty years for the church, and I do not
need to make a crust for one little pot pie on a Tuesday night.
This uses the other half of the cream of chicken from supper number one.
Here's what you need. Three quarters of a cup of cooked chicken, diced.
Half a cup of frozen mixed vegetables, the peas and carrots and corn and green beans.
Half a cup of condensed cream of chicken soup.
Two tablespoons of milk.
A pinch of pepper and a pinch of thyme.
And one refrigerated biscuit, from the tube. Once more. Three quarters
cup chicken. Half a cup frozen mixed vegetables. Half a cup cream of chicken.
Two tablespoons milk. Pepper and thyme. One biscuit. Heat your oven to four hundred.
In a small oven-safe bowl, or a
two-cup dish, stir together the soup and the milk,
then the chicken, the vegetables, the pepper and the thyme.
Now here's the trick, and it's important. The filling has to be hot when the biscuit goes
So put the bowl in the microwave for about two minutes, and stir
it, and then a little more, till it's bubbling hot. If the filling
is cold, the bottom of the biscuit stays raw and doughy.
Press the biscuit flat with your hand, a little bigger than it came out
of the tube, and lay it right on top of the hot filling.
Put the bowl on a small baking sheet, in case it bubbles over.
Bake fifteen to eighteen minutes, till the biscuit is tall and golden. And what do you do
biscuits in the tube? Bake them all at once, and freeze them in a bag. Or wrap the raw one
plastic, one at a time, and freeze them, and they're ready for the next pot pie. Look at t
A golden biscuit lid, with the gravy bubbling up around the edges.
Break into the top, and it's steaming.
About two dollars and thirty cents. That's a pot pie for one, and I didn't touch a rolling
Mix it up on Sunday, and keep it in the refrigerator in the
little dish, covered, for up to three days.
Then it's just heat it hot, biscuit on top, and bake.
A pot pie doesn't freeze well with the biscuit on top.
Freeze just the filling, if you want to, for two months.
§CH11§ And supper number seven is Swiss steak.
SHOTS.name: Swiss steak

SHOTS.txt: My mother made Swiss steak every Saturday night in the winter,
because it simmered on the back of the stove while she did the
ironing. And it's the cheapest piece of beef there is.
This uses the other half of the tomato soup. Here's what you need.
One cube steak, about a quarter pound. That's the one
at the meat counter with the little squares pressed into it.
One tablespoon of flour. Salt and pepper.
One teaspoon of oil.
A quarter of an onion, sliced. A quarter of a green
pepper, sliced, if you have one.
Half a can of condensed tomato soup. And a third of a cup of water.
Again. One cube steak. One tablespoon flour. Salt,
pepper. One teaspoon oil. A quarter onion. A quarter green
pepper. Half a can tomato soup. A third of a cup water.
Season the steak with salt and pepper, and press
it into the flour on both sides.
Heat the oil in your little skillet over medium-high heat, and
brown the steak about two minutes on each side.
Now put the onion and the pepper around the steak.
Stir the tomato soup and the water together in a cup, and pour it over everything.
Bring it to a bubble, then turn it down to low, put a lid
on, and let it simmer for thirty minutes.
Turn the steak once halfway through.
The long, slow simmer is what makes a tough cube steak fork tender.
It's also cooked well past a hundred and sixty, so you don't have to worry about it.
If the sauce gets too thick, add a spoonful of water.
And taste it at the end for salt. Look at that.
A tender steak in a red tomato gravy, with soft onions and peppers.
Over mashed potatoes, or egg noodles.
That's my mother's Saturday night.
About two dollars and fifty cents. Swiss steak freezes well, too, in its gravy. Let it coo
And when you warm it up, it's even more tender than the first night.
§CH12§ Now, those are the seven suppers. But some nights, honey, you want
soup as soup. So here are five ways I doctor up a can
of soup so it's a real supper, not a sad little bowl.
No card for these, just a spoon.
The first, a can of chicken noodle soup.
Add a half cup of cooked chicken, a handful of frozen peas and carrots,
and a few more egg noodles, and simmer it eight minutes.
One can just became two good bowls.
And a squeeze of lemon at the end.
The second, tomato soup.
Make it with milk instead of water, and float little squares
of grilled cheese sandwich on top, like croutons.
My grandson calls that a grilled cheese boat.
The third, vegetable beef.
Add a half cup of leftover pot roast or a little browned
ground beef, and a spoon of frozen corn.
Now it's stew.
The fourth, cheddar cheese soup.
Thin it with half a can of milk, and stir in a cup of
steamed broccoli and a little diced ham.
That's broccoli cheese soup, and it tastes like the restaurant kind.
And the fifth, cream of potato.
Add a little crumbled bacon, a handful of shredded cheddar, and some green onion.
It's loaded baked potato soup, for about a dollar.
§CH12A§ And one more, because some of you have asked me what I do for breakfast.
This is eggs goldenrod, and my mother made it for Easter morning.
It's creamed eggs on toast, and with a can of soup
it takes ten minutes. Here's what you need.
Two hard-cooked eggs. A third of a can of condensed cream of chicken soup. Three tablespoo
pinch of pepper. And one or two slices of toast. Again. Two hard-cooked eggs. A third of a
of cream of chicken. Three tablespoons milk. Pepper. Toast. Peel the eggs, and cut them in
Pop the yolks out and set them aside.

rice.title: Cheesy Chicken and Rice Skillet
ingredients: 1/2 can condensed cream of chicken soup
steps: Stir soup and milk in skillet, medium heat.
Add rice, chicken, peas. Heat till bubbling.
Season with pepper. Stir so rice doesn't stick.
Sprinkle cheese on top. Broil 2-3 minutes.
Let sit 2 minutes before eating.
rice.tip: Use an oven-safe skillet for broiling the cheese.

tuna.title: Tuna Noodle Casserole
ingredients: 1/2 can condensed cream of mushroom soup
steps: Cook noodles 6 minutes, drain.
Mix soup, milk, lemon juice till smooth.
Add tuna, peas, noodles. Stir gently.
Spoon in baking dish. Top with cheese, crackers.
Bake 20 minutes at 375°F, till bubbly.
tuna.tip: A little lemon juice brightens the whole dish.

hobo.title: Hamburger Hobo Packet
ingredients: 2 tbsp condensed cream of mushroom soup
steps: Layer potato, carrot, onion on foil.
Season, add patty, season again.
Top with soup and butter.
Fold foil tightly. Bake 40 minutes at 400°F.
Open carefully; watch for steam.
hobo.tip: Fold foil edges twice so steam stays in.

goulash.title: Goulash
steps: Brown beef and onion in skillet.
Add soup, water, seasoning. Bubble 3 minutes.
Add macaroni. Simmer 2 minutes.
Turn off heat, top with cheese.
Cover 1 minute to melt cheese.
goulash.tip: Add green pepper or corn for variety.

pork.title: Smothered Pork Chop
ingredients: 1/2 can condensed cream of mushroom soup
steps: Season and brown chop 3 minutes per side.
Remove chop. Cook onion 4 minutes.
Stir in soup and milk till smooth.
Return chop, cover, simmer 8-10 minutes.
Rest 3 minutes before serving.
pork.tip: A pork chop is done at 145°F in the middle.

potpie.title: Chicken Pot Pie with Biscuit Lid
ingredients: 1/2 cup condensed cream of chicken soup
steps: Mix soup, milk, chicken, veggies, pepper, thyme.
Heat filling till bubbling hot.
Flatten biscuit, place on hot filling.
Bake 15-18 minutes at 400°F.
Let cool slightly before eating.
potpie.tip: Heat filling hot before adding biscuit so it cooks through.

swiss.title: Swiss Steak
steps: Season steak, press into flour.
Brown steak in oil, 2 minutes per side.
Add onion, pepper. Pour soup and water over.
Simmer covered 30 minutes, turning once.
Add water if sauce thickens too much.
swiss.tip: Long, slow simmer makes cube steak fork tender.

sauce.title: Homemade Cream-of Soup
steps: Melt butter, stir in flour, cook 1 minute.
Whisk in broth, then milk, no lumps.
Bubble 3-4 minutes till thick.
Season with salt and pepper.
Cool and store in jar for 3 days.
sauce.tip: Add mushrooms or celery for other soup flavors.

bfast.title: Goldenrod Eggs Breakfast
ingredients: 1/3 can condensed cream of chicken soup
steps: Peel eggs, separate yolks, chop whites.
Heat soup and milk till smooth and hot.
Stir in chopped whites and pepper.
Pour over toast on plate.
Crumble yolks on top for goldenrod look.
bfast.tip: Hard-cooked eggs keep a week in the fridge.

extra.title: Tomato Soup Spice Cake (Grandmother's)
steps: Mix dry ingredients in bowl.
Beat shortening, soup, egg, water together.
Stir dry into wet, add raisins.
Pour in greased 8x4 loaf pan.
Bake 40-45 minutes at 350°F.
extra.tip: A little cream cheese frosting is wonderful on top.
